item.title: Growth Vs Profitability: Swiggy’s Tug-Of-War
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: Swiggy’s results for the second quarter (Q2) of the financial year 2026-27 (FY27) show that the tug of war between…
item.content:encoded:
Swiggy’s results for the second quarter (Q2) of the financial year 2026-27 (FY27) show that the tug of war between growth and profitability is intensifying, as Instamart’s mounting losses threaten to overshadow the improving performance of its food-delivery business.

On October 23, 2026, the company’s shares fell around 15% to ₹179.90 on the BSE, wiping out roughly ₹9,000 Cr in market capitalisation in a single session. The sell-off came after Swiggy reported its results, with widening losses at Instamart overshadowing improving profitability in its food delivery business. The stock has also lost more than half its value since its market debut in November 2024. 

The company’s revenue from operations increased 36.1% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr in the September quarter. Its consolidated net loss narrowed to ₹922 Cr from ₹1,092 Cr a year earlier, but widened from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. 

The contrast within the business is becoming more pronounced. Food delivery reported record adjusted EBITDA, supported by advertising revenue and delivery efficiencies. Instamart, meanwhile, saw its adjusted EBITDA loss widen to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier, even as its net order value (NOV) grew 13.4% sequentially.

This has put investors in a spot, questioning whether Swiggy’s rising investments today can deliver sustainable returns tomorrow. Or will the coming quarters reveal whether Instamart’s renewed growth can translate into better margins? But before that…

Instamart’s Growth Comes At A Cost

Instamart’s Q2 numbers show a recovery in growth momentum, but not yet a corresponding improvement in profitability. The business’s net order value (NOV) rose 13.4% QoQ to ₹6,594 Cr in Q2 FY27 against 2.5% growth in the preceding quarter. Orders rose 29.3% YoY to 130 Mn. Instamart added 1.3 Mn monthly transacting users during the quarter, taking its user base to 14.8 Mn, up 23% YoY.

These are meaningful signs of demand. Management has also pointed to higher order frequency and stronger retention in the earnings call as evidence that Instamart is building shopping habits rather than relying solely on one-off purchases. Its strategy is to deepen engagement through everyday categories such as fresh produce and staples, while using differentiated assortment to give customers reasons to return.

However, customer and order growth are only one side of the story. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr in Q2 FY27, while its contribution margin deteriorated. According to the foodtech’s shareholders’ letter, Instamart reported a contribution margin of -1.0% of gross order value (GOV). The number suggests that the business is still spending heavily to attract and retain customers, fulfil orders and build out its network.

“This creates a difficult trade-off. Promotions and pricing investments can help drive orders, while more stores can improve proximity and delivery speed. But both require capital and operating expenditure. Unless higher order volumes, better monetisation and denser delivery networks improve the economics of each order, growth can continue to increase the absolute loss,” an industry source said.

The Swiggy management believes Instamart’s customer cohorts are becoming more productive and that differentiated assortment can improve retention over time. The company is also working to increase revenue per order through product mix, private labels and advertising, while reducing costs through network densification, automation and operating leverage.

The break-even ambition, however, remains elusive. Management has said Instamart needs to reach roughly 2.3X its current scale, with annualised NOV of around ₹60,000 Cr against approximately ₹26,400 Cr at present, alongside a contribution of about ₹30 per order. Swiggy estimates that roughly two-thirds of the improvement needed would come from higher revenue per order and the remainder from lower costs per order.

This is a roadmap rather than a near-term result. The company has not been able to give a detailed timeline for reaching break-even or quantify how much each lever would contribute. Investors will, therefore, need to look beyond headline growth and track whether contribution margin, order economics and adjusted EBITDA improve together.

Management expects double-digit sequential NOV growth in Q3 and an improvement of around 100 basis points in adjusted EBITDA margin QoQ. This makes the next quarter an important juncture.

Blinkit Raises The Bar For Instamart

Instamart’s challenge is not simply to grow. It has to build a network capable of competing with Blinkit while improving the economics of that expansion.

The difference in store footprint is also considerable. Instamart added 69 net dark stores in Q2 FY27, taking its total to 1,240 across 133 cities. Blinkit added 308 stores during the same quarter, taking its network to 2,751. Blinkit’s network is now more than twice the size of Instamart’s.

Scale matters in quick commerce because it affects how close a platform can be to customers, how efficiently it can fulfil orders and how much volume it can route through its network. A larger footprint can also provide more opportunities to improve availability and spread certain operating costs. But store count alone does not establish which business has better economics: store maturity, order density, basket size, local competition and the cost of operating each location all matter.

The financial contrast in Q2 is also stark. Blinkit reported positive adjusted EBITDA of ₹184 Cr, compared with Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹895 Cr. Blinkit’s NOV grew 22.2% sequentially, ahead of Instamart’s 13.4% growth. 

Eternal’s management has cited store paybacks and lower competitive intensity in Tier II markets, while maintaining its FY29 EBITDA ambition for Blinkit. In contrast, Swiggy has emphasised building customer habits, improving retention and developing its existing Tier I and II network. 

Instamart’s management did not commit to a new accelerated expansion plan in the earnings call, suggesting the near-term focus is on making the existing network more productive rather than simply matching Blinkit store for store.

“There is a reasonable case for this approach. Adding stores without sufficient local demand can dilute returns, and a smaller network can still be productive if it generates enough orders per location. But restraint also carries a risk: a weaker physical footprint can limit reach and availability in a market where speed and convenience are central to the proposition,” the executive quoted above said.

Therefore, the key question is whether Instamart can close the gap through better throughput, assortment and monetisation, rather than relying primarily on expansion. 

Swiggy’s shareholder letter also points to a planned transition to an inventory-led model, under which Instamart would own the inventory it sells. Management expects this to improve contribution margin by around 80 basis points and shorten the working-capital cycle. The transition is expected to begin mid-Q3 FY27 and take two to three quarters to complete.

What Can Support Swiggy’s Valuation?

Swiggy’s market fall also reflects the tension between a relatively stronger food delivery business and a quick commerce operation that continues to consume substantial resources.

Food delivery GOV grew 17.7% YoY to ₹10,054 Cr in Q2 FY27. Adjusted EBITDA increased 42% to ₹341 Cr, with the adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 3.4% from 2.8% a year ago. Higher advertising revenue and delivery efficiencies supported the performance. 

This business provides an important counterweight to Instamart’s losses. Its profitability shows that Swiggy can generate operating earnings from an established marketplace, even as it continues to invest in newer businesses. It also gives the company a base from which to fund growth.

The difficulty is that stronger food-delivery performance has not yet offset the pressure from Instamart. Swiggy’s consolidated net loss widened sequentially, and analysts have questioned whether its quick commerce growth is keeping pace with expectations. 

Citi, for instance, noted that Instamart’s sequential NOV growth was below its estimate, while its adjusted EBITDA loss was higher than expected. CLSA also flagged slower-than-expected growth and wider losses, while other brokerages have lowered price targets amid concerns about execution and the time required to reach profitability. 

This, however, does not mean that Instamart’s growth strategy cannot work. Quick commerce requires upfront investment in stores, inventory, customer acquisition and logistics, and some of those costs may become more efficient as order density improves. The issue is how long investors should be expected to wait for those benefits.

Therefore, Swiggy’s immediate task is to show that Q2 was a turning point in loss trajectory, as management expects, rather than another quarter in which growth came at a higher cost. The next set of results will need to show sustained sequential NOV growth alongside improving contribution and adjusted EBITDA margins. Customer additions will matter, but so will repeat ordering, store productivity and the extent to which revenue per order rises.

The inventory-led transition will be another milestone to watch. For now, as Swiggy continues to get stuck in a tug-of-war between profitability and growth, its market fall is a reminder that revenue growth alone is unlikely to reassure investors.

Can Zetwerk Turn Thin Margins Into Profits? The company made its stock market debut amid strong manufacturing tailwinds, but thin margins and rising cash outflows pose challenges. Despite 40.4% revenue growth to ₹15,913 Cr in FY26, its net loss widened to ₹1,606 Cr, raising questions about whether scale can deliver sustainable profitability.

Unicommerce Q2 Profit Rises 11% YoY: The ecommerce SaaS company reported an 11% YoY rise in Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹6.4 Cr, while revenue grew 15% to ₹59.1 Cr. Adjusted EBITDA margin stood at 17%, as the company added 121 enterprise clients and expects profitability to improve in H2 as investments moderate.

Bluestone Slips Into Losses: The omnichannel jewellery retailer reported a ₹4.4 Cr net loss in Q2 FY27, compared with a ₹6 Cr profit in the preceding quarter, even as revenue surged 45% YoY to ₹745 Cr. Adjusted PAT turned positive at ₹19.6 Cr, while the retailer expanded its network to 379 stores.

Eternal Q2 Profit Jumps 92%: The foodtech giant reported a 92% YoY jump in Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹125 Cr, while operating revenue surged 78% to ₹24,138 Cr. Blinkit’s revenue grew 94%, with its store count reaching 2,751, while Zomato’s food delivery growth regained pace and Hyperpure turned EBITDA positive.

item.title: Flipkart’s Summer Of Discontent
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: Questions over an IPO and ESOPs, huge investments in quick commerce and food delivery and the pressure to deliver profits:…
item.content:encoded:
Questions over an IPO and ESOPs, huge investments in quick commerce and food delivery and the pressure to deliver profits: Flipkart is juggling one too many hot potatoes for the past year. 

In that time, the ecommerce giant has seen 14 senior level exits, including three more VPs who are set to leave the company next. 

The latest executives to leave are Kanchan Mishra, VP of smartphones; Amit Sachan, VP of product and tech; and Kamal Chopra, VP of corporate, as Moneycontrol reported. While Mishra spent more than a decade at Flipkart, Sachan and Chopra have been with the company for four and five years, respectively. 

As their tenure shows these are not employees who had just joined the company one or two years ago in the wake of all the IPO talk. These were executives who had seen much of the restructuring at Flipkart in the post-pandemic years.   

Plus, these departures come at a time when the company’s employees have raised concerns over ESOP liquidity and the company’s long-awaited IPO remains without a firm timeline. It has coloured these exits with a darker tint as a result. 

Walmart has reportedly asked the company to prioritise profitability before going public, while the expansion of its quick commerce business, Flipkart Minutes, requires significant ongoing investments. Employees holding stock options, meanwhile, are waiting for an opportunity to cash out. 

Sources told Inc42 that some of these executives left as they were unable to see a clear opportunity to liquidate their ESOPs, while others moved to new jobs or wanted to start their own ventures. It must be noted that at this middle management level, Flipkart has around 30 executives in VP roles and more than a dozen senior vice presidents, so these departures will not necessarily destabilise the company, but it is a sign of bubbling discontent.   

ESOP Liquidity Dispute Widens 

In fact, sources told us that the frustration over stock options has moved beyond internal discussions, with former senior executives approaching Walmart’s board to seek a fair opportunity to realise the value of their vested ESOPs.

Earlier this month, former Flipkart executives, including ex-Myntra CEO Mukesh Bansal, former chief business officer Ankit Nagori and former CFO Sanjay Baweja, wrote to Walmart’s board seeking fair treatment and a full cash-out opportunity for their vested options simply because they left the company. 

The issue has gained importance because an IPO has long been seen as a potential exit route for employees holding Flipkart shares or options. With the listing pushed back, those employees have little clarity on when they can realise that value. 

For senior executives who have spent a year at Flipkart, the delay also affects decisions about whether to stay or pursue opportunities elsewhere. While ESOP liquidity is one reason behind some departures, the company’s leadership churn is also a result of executives moving into new roles or setting up their own ventures. 

The founder of a unicorn startup with over 30,000 employees told us that while Flipkart has the responsibility of providing liquidity to employees, listing in a hurry to meet these demands would be a mistake. 

“At the end of the day, Flipkart’s management and Walmart have to do the right thing by the company. If they have already done a $50 Mn ESOP buy back last year, then they already provided some liquidity opportunity. If an employee has already made ₹10 Cr – ₹15 Cr through that, then they need to give the company some more time for the next event. But if an employee who has made a few lakhs of rupees via the buyback is upset, then the management needs to address that. What’s the point of listing in a rush, without getting a good market value?” the founder said on the condition of anonymity. 

Walmart Wants Profit Before IPO

The fact is that Flipkart’s listing plans have been discussed for years, but the immediate priority appears to be improving its financial performance.

In May 2026, Moneycontrol reported that parent Walmart wanted Flipkart to achieve EBITDA breakeven by the end of FY27 before considering an IPO or another external fundraise. The report said the decision followed Walmart CEO John Furner’s visit to Bengaluru. 

The reported directive adds another hurdle for a company that completed its reverse flip from Singapore to India in March 2026, ahead of a potential domestic listing. 

There is the looming valuation question. Flipkart currently commands a valuation of $35 Bn – $36 Bn and earlier was eyeing a valuation of $50 Bn. 

This valuation expectation complicates finding the right window for the listing. Walmart can afford to wait for improved financial performance which would justify the valuation, but that’s not the case with employees seeking liquidity. 

“In a current situation, getting a $50 Bn valuation will be extremely difficult. It is indeed a tricky position for the company,” the founder quoted above added. 

Others believe that Flipkart cannot go into an IPO with the narrative of a growth-at-all-costs tech startup. The company is far too mature for this. “Flipkart will likely face pushback and could be forced into a valuation haircut to land in the $25B–$30 Bn range. This will match global tech-retail multiples,” Rahul Sharma, Head of Research at Equity99 said.

On the other hand, the company can position itself as a disciplined, maturing omnichannel ecosystem. “A concrete roadmap to profitability can successfully defend the $35 Bn mark that Flipkart is said to be seeking,” he added.  

The delay is particularly striking because other Indian ecommerce companies have already reached the public markets. Meesho listed on the NSE and BSE on December 10, 2025, following a ₹5,421 Cr IPO. Snapdeal’s parent, AceVector, listed on October 5, 2026, after a ₹420 Cr public issue. 

Their listing gives investors a way to set benchmarks for ecommerce, while Flipkart continues to work towards its own debut. However, the comparison also shows that going public does guarantee a strong market reception. AceVector shares listed at an issue price of ₹32 and subsequently traded below that level.

For Flipkart, the question is whether stronger financial performance can support  its valuation expectations without forcing the company to slow its growth plans. 

Flipkart Minutes Complicates Profitability Push

The push to improve profitability comes amid Flipkart’s aggressive investments in quick commerce.

Flipkart Minutes has expanded its dark store network to compete with Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto. The business gives Flipkart a way to serve customers looking for rapid delivery of groceries, electronics and other everyday products. 

However, the expansion requires spending on dark stores, inventory, fulfillment and delivery operations. New stores need time to build order volumes and improve their economics. Until a store reaches sufficient throughput, its operating costs can weigh on the business. Flipkart Minutes has scaled to 1,000 micro fulfillment centers across 130+ cities and 8,000+ pincodes in under two years.

The current scale of Minutes’ spending is not publicly disclosed. However, its expansion presents a challenge for Flipkart as Walmart reportedly seeks EBITDA breakeven before an IPO.

Now, Flipkart is preparing to enter another competitive market with its food delivery service branded eat-in by Minutes. Currently available for its 8,000 employees, will soon be available to the public by the end of this month. 

The food delivery business could add to Flipkart’s spending requirements. The company reportedly will use a dedicated delivery fleet through its logistics arm Ekart. 

Moreover, it will also require onboard restaurants and attract customers in a market where established players spend on discounts, promotions and customer acquisition. These costs could build before the service reaches sufficient order volumes to support its operations. 

The launch puts Flipkart in the position of investing in two businesses that require scale to improve their economics, even as Walmart reportedly wants the group to reach EBITDA breakeven before an IPO. While food delivery could bring more frequent customer visits to Flipkart’s app, it will also require spending to compete with established platforms. 

Losses Grow, Pressure Builds

Flipkart’s financial performance will also remain under scrutiny as it works towards a potential IPO. 

The Flipkart Group reported an 18.2% YoY increase in consolidated revenue from operation to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr in FY26, compared with ₹1.23 Lakh Cr in FY25. Its consolidated net loss narrowed marginally by 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr from ₹8,646 Cr in the previous year.   The financial results cover the wider Flipkart Group, including Myntra, Cleartrip, logistics, and other business, rather than the ecommerce marketplace alone. 

The group said its gross margins rose 23% during FY26, while adjusted EBITDA improved by around ₹1,500 Cr. Adjusted operating margin improved by 230 basis points, from -7.7% to -5.4%, while adjusted operating business losses narrowed by 17%, or around ₹1,600 Cr. 

However, the improvement in operating performance translated into only a modest reduction in net loss. Higher finance cost, the recognition of deferred tax assets and certain exceptional items weighed on the bottom line. 

The ecommerce vertical, Flipkart Internet, reported a 19.3% YoY decline in revenue from operations to ₹16,295 Cr in FY26. Its net loss rose to ₹5,498 Cr from ₹1,694 Cr in FY25. A significant portion of that is likely due to the redomiciling to India which was completed in March 2026. 

As Flipkart works on its public market plans, the combination of profitability targets, valuation expectations and employee concerns over stock liquidity is likely to remain in focus. For senior executives weighing their next move, the absence of a firm IPO timeline leaves questions unanswered: when will the equity they have accumulated at Flipkart become liquid wealth?

item.title: New-Age Tech Stocks Tumble This Week, Swiggy Leads Sell-Off With 24.5% Fall
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: New-age tech stocks lost over $11 Bn in combined market capitalisation this week, with Swiggy leading a broad sell-off amid…
item.content:encoded:
New-age tech stocks lost over $11 Bn in combined market capitalisation this week, with Swiggy leading a broad sell-off amid weakness in the wider Indian equity market.

Of the 67 stocks under Inc42’s coverage before this week’s listings, 63 declined between 1.03% and 24.5%. Only Yudiz, Capillary, ixigo, and Tracxn ended the week higher.

Swiggy was the biggest loser, falling 24.5% to close at ₹176.70 after its Q2 FY27 results highlighted mounting losses at quick commerce arm Instamart. The stock touched an all-time low during intraday trade yesterday. 

Twelve other stocks, including Yatra, Turtlemint, FirstCry, Unicommerce, and IndiaMART InterMESH, hit fresh 52-week lows during the holiday-shortened week.

The selling extended to Eternal, Ola Electric, Paytm, and Lenskart, dragging the combined market capitalisation of the 67 companies to $149.2 Bn.

Meanwhile, B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk and defence tech company Tonbo Imaging made their public market debuts at a premium yesterday. Both came under pressure after listing, closing 13.02% and 2.44% below their respective BSE listing prices.

The two additions took the combined market capitalisation of the 69 new-age tech stocks tracked by Inc42 to $152.32 Bn, equivalent to about 3.2% of the total market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies.

Here are some of the key developments at listed new-age tech companies during the week.

Eternal Reports Profit Jump

Eternal reported a nearly 92% YoY jump in Q2 FY27 net profit and unveiled Dark, an end-to-end encrypted AI platform for advanced AI users. Founder Deepinder Goyal said a global launch is planned before the end of 2026.

Eternal also announced a proposed merger between portfolio company AdOnMo and gated-community management platform Mygate. It expects to hold a 4.4% stake in the merged entity.

Ecommerce Platforms Face Action

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) took action against seven ecommerce platforms, including IndiaMART and Justdial, over listings and sales of unauthorised hazardous explosives.

The action led to the removal of 3,940 sellers and product listings across the platforms.

ideaForge Terminates US Agreement

Drone maker ideaForge’s wholly owned US subsidiary terminated its joint venture agreement with US-based First Breach Inc, citing the failure to complete the transaction within the agreed deadline and discussions between the parties.

Signed on September 23, 2025, the agreement envisaged a joint venture to license, source, design, engineer, manufacture, and distribute unmanned aerial vehicles in the US.

Unicommerce Logs Profit Growth

Ecommerce SaaS company Unicommerce’s consolidated net profit rose 11% YoY to ₹6.4 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue grew 15% to ₹59.1 Cr. Expenses increased 19%, outpacing revenue growth, with a lower tax expense supporting profit growth. The company expects profitability to improve in H2 as incremental investments moderate.

With that, here’s a look at the broader market trend this week.

Markets End Winning Streak

The Sensex declined 2.15% to 73,123.83, while the Nifty 50 fell 2.63% to 22,600 during the week.

Both indices declined across all four trading sessions, with markets closed on Tuesday for Dussehra. Rising crude prices, geopolitical tensions in West Asia, and sustained FII outflows weighed on sentiment.

Broader markets saw steeper falls. The Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 declined 5.6% and 7.3%, respectively, while the Nifty Bank lost 2.8%.

Brent crude approaching $115 per barrel heightened concerns over inflation, rupee depreciation, and corporate margins. Investors also scrutinised Q2 earnings, valuations, and management guidance. IT stocks remained relatively resilient, while metals, realty, and consumer durables faced selling pressure.

Foreign investors sold equities worth ₹2,697 Cr, their tenth consecutive week of net selling, although outflows moderated from ₹8,991 Cr. Domestic institutional investors bought ₹10,942 Cr.

“Going ahead, the steady moderation in FII selling offers some comfort, though elevated crude and sharp broader-market weakness keep the downside risk alive,” said Vinod Nair, head of research at Geojit Investments.

Next week, investors will track Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan rate decisions, US GDP, India’s industrial production, and corporate earnings. West Asia developments, crude prices, US treasury yields, and India-US trade negotiations will also remain in focus.

Now, let’s take a look at the performance of Swiggy and ixigo. 

ixigo Defies Market Sell-Off

ixigo rose 1.45% during the week following its Q2 results on October 17.

The online travel aggregator swung to a consolidated net profit of ₹63.4 Cr from a ₹3.5 Cr loss a year earlier. This included a ₹40.7 Cr exceptional gain from the partial sale of its Freshbus stake and remeasurement of its remaining investment.

Operating revenue grew 12.9% YoY to ₹321 Cr, while gross transaction value (GTV) rose 22% to ₹5,304.5 Cr. However, adjusted EBITDA fell 17.2% to ₹23.6 Cr, with the margin narrowing to 7.3% from 10%.

Hotel GTV surged 158.7% to ₹111.3 Cr, while revenue increased to ₹8.1 Cr from ₹1.3 Cr. Room nights exceeded 4.7 Lakh, and inventory topped 70,000 properties. However, the segment’s contribution loss widened to ₹1.2 Cr from ₹71 Lakh.

Train revenue increased 16.4% to ₹149.1 Cr, while bus revenue rose 23.8% to ₹81 Cr. Flight revenue fell 7.5% to ₹82.7 Cr despite 37.2% GTV growth, with the gross take rate declining to 7% from 9.38%.

Choice Equity retained its ‘ADD’ rating and ₹190 target, citing hotel growth but flagging margin pressure from planned investments of ₹10-12 Cr over the next couple of quarters.

Swiggy Hits Record Low

Swiggy’s 24.5% weekly fall left it 54.7% below its ₹390 IPO price, with widening Instamart losses weighing on sentiment.

Its consolidated Q2 FY27 loss narrowed 16% YoY to ₹922 Cr but widened 17% sequentially from ₹791 Cr. Operating revenue rose 36% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr, while consumer-facing businesses’ gross order value (GOV) increased 25% to ₹20,793 Cr.

Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier and ₹778 Cr in Q1, despite GOV rising 31% YoY to ₹9,230 Cr.

Swiggy cited pricing investments, customer and category mix changes, and new dark-store costs for contribution-margin pressure. It expects Q2 to mark peak adjusted EBITDA losses and anticipates around 100 basis points of margin improvement in Q3.

Food delivery’s adjusted EBITDA rose to a record ₹341 Cr from ₹240 Cr, while revenue grew 22% to ₹2,338 Cr. Segment profit increased 39% to ₹349 Cr.

Swiggy plans to shift Instamart to an inventory-led model over two to three quarters, targeting an 80-basis-point contribution-margin improvement.

Brokerages largely retained ratings but cut targets over quick commerce losses and execution concerns. HSBC lowered its target to ₹240 from ₹315, while CLSA cut its target to ₹262.

item.title: Myntra Slips Into The Red In FY26, Reports ₹582 Cr Loss
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Fashion ecommerce platform Myntra reported a net loss of ₹581.8 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26),…
item.content:encoded:
Fashion ecommerce platform Myntra reported a net loss of ₹581.8 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26), reversing a net profit of ₹546.3 Cr in the previous fiscal.

Myntra’s operating revenue fell 13.5% to ₹5,242.5 Cr in the fiscal under review, compared to ₹6,063.8 Cr in FY25. Myntra earns revenue from three streams – marketplace services, logistics services and advertisement services. 

Breaking down the top line, marketplace and collection services contributed to 50.7%. It stood at ₹2,657.3 Cr in FY26, marking a 3% increase from ₹2,580.2 Cr in the previous year. Advertisement Services rose 35.2% to ₹1,236.4 Cr in the year under review, from ₹914.5 Cr in FY25.

Meanwhile, logistics and shipping services fell 53.2% to ₹1,119.2 Cr in FY2025-26, from ₹2,390.5 Cr a year ago. Besides these, other operating revenue contributed ₹229.6 Cr, taking the overall topline to ₹5,242.5 Cr in the reported year.

Including other income of ₹73.3 Cr, the total income for the fiscal year FY26 stood at ₹5,315.8 Cr, a 13.4% fall from ₹6,137 Cr.

The company’s EBITDA loss stood at ₹435 Cr in FY26, from ₹535.9 Cr in FY25.

Founded in 2007 by Mukesh Bansal, Ashutosh Lawania and Vineet Saxena, Myntra is an online marketplace which allows third-party sellers to sell their fashion products. The Bengaluru-based startup was acquired by Flipkart for $240 Mn in 2014.

“Flipkart Group is made up of various business verticals, including Flipkart, Myntra, and Cleartrip. Stakeholders should refer to the consolidated financials of Flipkart Internet Private Limited (Consolidated) when assessing the Flipkart Group’s overall financial performance over the reporting period,” Flipkart said in a statement.

Earlier this year, Flipkart Fashion’s Sharon Pais was elevated to the role of the head of fashion marketplace arm Myntra, replacing Nandita Sinha. Additionally, Myntra also appointed Instacart executive Pramod Adiddam as its chief technology officer (CTO).

Myntra’s parent, Flipkart Group, also released its consolidated FY26 financials following its reverse flip to India. The Walmart-backed ecommerce group saw an 18.2% jump in consolidated revenue from operations to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr while loss narrowed 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr.

“At the PAT level, net loss reduced by approximately ₹180 Cr year over year. The improvement was moderated by higher finance costs, the derecognition of deferred tax assets recognised in earlier periods and certain one-off exceptional items,” the company said in a blog post.

Zooming Into Myntra’s FY26 Expenses

Total expenses for the year 2025-26 remained nearly flat, with a 0.6% increase to ₹5,757.7 Cr, from ₹5,726 Cr in the previous year. Here is a closer look at where the ecommerce platform spent the most:

  • Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenses towards salaries, wages, bonus, staff welfare, gratuity and provident fund, Myntra spent ₹776.9 Cr in the year under review, up 3.8% from ₹748.8 Cr in FY25.
  • Direct Expenses: Constituting 32% of the total expenses, this includes payment gateway charges and logistic charges. Direct expenses stood at ₹1,841 Cr, marking a 13.9% decline from ₹2,139.4 Cr. 
  • Advertisement And Promotion Expenses: Spending under this head rose 10.5% to ₹2,326.5 Cr, compared to ₹2,105.3 Cr, contributing 40.4% of the overall expenditure.

item.content:encoded:
UPI provider super.money reported a net loss of ₹263.8 Cr in FY26, 78.5% higher than ₹147.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal year. 

Its operating revenue more than tripled to ₹292.4 Cr from ₹88.8 Cr in FY25. Its loan marketplace contributed around 84.7% of its revenue. 

Combined with other income of ₹90 Lakh, its total income amounted to ₹293.3 Cr. super.money did not report any tax expenses or exceptional items, resulting in a total comprehensive loss of ₹262.9 Cr. 

super.money was launched by the Walmart-owned Flipkart in 2024 and is led by founder and CEO Prakash Sikaria, who was the senior vice president at Flipkart, helming its ads business, Shopsy, Cleartrip and Yantra.

super.money’s core business is enabling UPI payments and is the fifth largest player in the market. In September 2026, it processed over 40.51 Cr UPI transactions, collectively worth more than ₹19,613.3 Cr. 

Besides, the startup has now also ventured into loan facilitation, connecting borrowers with banks and NBFCs. It also enables users to book fixed deposits and partners with banks to offer co-branded credit cards. 

Where Did super.money Spend?

super.money’s total expenses in FY26 surged 130% YoY to ₹557.1 Cr from ₹241.8 Cr in the previous fiscal. Let’s dive into a breakdown of its spending. 

  • Business Promotion Expenses: This was the biggest expenditure, rising 3.34X YoY to ₹341 Cr in FY26. 
  • Employee Benefits Expense: Employee costs grew 73.8% YoY to ₹138.1 Cr compared to ₹79.5 Cr in the year-ago period. 
  • Marketplace Charges: Spending on this line item fell 64.2% YoY to ₹15.6 Cr from ₹43.5 Cr. 
  • Finance Costs: super.money’s finance-related expenses skyrocketed to ₹11.1 Cr in the year under review from ₹0.1 Cr in the previous year. 
  • Other Expenses: Other operating expenses including outside contracted services and communication charges increased 177.2% YoY to ₹47.9 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹17.3 Cr in FY25.

item.title: PHP2Shell: Who Is At Risk And How Can Businesses Stay Safe?
item.dc:creator: Ankush Das
item.description: PHP, a programming language used to build websites, is at the centre of a major security concern after researchers uncovered…
item.content:encoded:
PHP, a programming language used to build websites, is at the centre of a major security concern after researchers uncovered two critical flaws that could let hackers take control of vulnerable servers.

Called PHP2Shell, the vulnerabilities could let attackers run malicious code on affected systems without needing to log in. Since the vulnerabilities lie in PHP itself rather than individual websites built on it, businesses cannot rely on website-level security measures alone to stay protected.

The vulnerabilities affect specific PHP versions, and fixes were released on October 21, 2026. Businesses must now check whether they are running affected versions, install the updates and investigate whether hackers exploited the flaws before the fixes were applied.

The discovery story involves both independent research and AI-assisted security work. Security firm Calif credited pseudonymous researcher LCFR with first discovering PHP2Shell and developing a working exploit. Separately, AI company OpenAI said security research firm Calif identified a critical flaw using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, while cybersecurity firm Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. OpenAI’s disclosure describes the collaboration that helped prepare fixes before public disclosure.

The episode also highlights a growing cybersecurity concern: AI tools are helping researchers uncover complex security flaws, but organisations must be equally agile to fix them.

Which Businesses Face The Risk?

PHP powers around 70% of websites globally. This highlights the language’s reach, but does not mean that 70% of websites are vulnerable. The actual risk depends on the PHP version, server configuration and exposure to attack. The vulnerabilities can allow attackers to run code remotely on affected servers without authentication.

Amruta Moktali, chief product officer at Skyflow, a data privacy and security platform, said initial industry reports cited millions of potentially exposed instances because PHP is widely used across websites, content management systems, hosting environments and enterprise applications.

For Indian businesses, Moktali said the immediate priority should be internet-facing PHP systems that handle sensitive information. These include systems connected to payment services, customer databases and identity and authentication tools.

Small businesses and website operators may face additional challenges if they depend on third-party hosting providers or lack dedicated security teams. They may not know which PHP version their websites use or whether their provider has installed the relevant updates.

Sooraj Sathyanarayanan, a cybersecurity researcher and program manager at privacy-focused web browser Brave, said successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute code without logging in or requiring user interaction. Depending on the server’s permissions, this could expose customer data and credentials, enable website changes or allow malware to be installed.

However, the level of risk depends on the PHP build and server configuration, so not all installations are equally vulnerable.

Legacy systems are another concern, as the flaw occurs within PHP’s core engine before an application’s own code runs.

“One thing organisations must keep in mind with PHP2Shell is that because this flaw triggers inside the core PHP engine before any application code executes, traditional application-level safeguards won’t stop it,” said Niv Lanyado, security research team lead for PHP at JFrog, a software supply chain security company.

He stressed that organisations need visibility into all their systems, particularly older PHP installations that may no longer receive security updates, so they can be patched or isolated.

Fixing The Software Is Not Enough

The PHP team released fixed versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 on October 21. Its official security advisory says there are no complete mitigations and urges users to update.

Organisations should first identify where PHP is running across their servers, cloud environments and third-party hosting arrangements. They should then check which installations are affected and confirm that the updated software is active.

According to Aditya Narayana K, the cofounder of cybersecurity company focused on AI security, Mirror Security, organisations need a repeatable process to identify vulnerabilities, fix them and verify that the fixes work. He pointed to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 as a useful guide for managing this process.

“Organisations must confirm that patches are active and the vulnerability is no longer reproducible, rather than assuming that applying a patch resolves the risk,” Narayana said.

Where immediate patching is not possible, businesses should follow official guidance from PHP and their hosting or software providers. Temporary measures may reduce exposure, but they are not a substitute for a complete fix. Unsupported installations may need to be upgraded or isolated until they can be secured. 

The incident has also raised questions about whether businesses can keep pace with AI-assisted vulnerability discovery. 

Sriram Krishnan, a technology investor and former general partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), wrote on X that the PHP disclosure will make the ecosystem safer by finding long-lurking issues.  “However, the entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes. We might need a lot more public + private partnerships to secure infrastructure across the country.”

How Can Businesses Check For A Breach?

Patching closes a known vulnerability, but it does not establish whether hackers exploited it before the update was installed. Businesses must investigate their past exposure alongside fixing their systems.

According to Narayana of Mirror Security, investigators should identify which systems were exposed and review activity from before patching. This includes checking server logs, unusual system behaviour, unauthorised file changes and suspicious network connections.

Organisations should also look for unexpected programs running on their servers or unexplained changes to files and configurations. Security teams can use monitoring tools to bring together information from different systems and identify patterns that may indicate an attack.

Sathyanarayanan recommended reviewing activity from at least a week before the October 21 patch release, given that exploitation attempts were reported before public disclosure. Businesses should not assume that installing a fix eliminates the risk of an earlier compromise.

If investigators find signs of an attack, they should preserve logs and other evidence, involve their hosting provider or an incident response specialist, and assess whether credentials need to be replaced. Patching alone may not remove malicious software or unauthorised access established before the fix.

An attempted attack does not necessarily mean hackers gained access. Equally, the absence of security alerts does not guarantee that a system is safe.

Timely patching must go hand in hand with continuous security monitoring, as attackers can move quickly once vulnerability details become public. The PHP2Shell disclosure demonstrates why cybersecurity cannot end with a software update. Businesses need to know what technology they run, fix vulnerabilities quickly and establish whether attackers gained access before the fix was applied.

As AI tools make it easier to uncover complex flaws, the ability to investigate, patch and verify systems quickly will become just as important as discovering the vulnerabilities themselves.

For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now.

For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation.

Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, PRISM, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses.

The list also includes Indian companies like MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, which are listed on Nasdaq in the US.

India’s startup IPO wave reached its peak in 2025, surpassing the previous year’s momentum.

Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride

Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. 

While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges.

While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. Over 60 of the new-age tech companies are currently profitable.

In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. 

It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s purview are about a decade old. 

From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra’s IPO materialised within four years of its operations.  

Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal.

Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr

Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom

The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem.

The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups.

While fintech and ecommerce house 14 names each, 13 enterprise tech startups have listed on the bourses so far. 

The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of Tonbo Imaging, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts.

Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups

While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 27 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru’s ninetineen and Mumbai’s fifteen. 

While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. 

Delhi NCR contributes $90 Bn in the cumulative $167 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies.

item.title: Festive Sales See Shoppers Log In But Hold Back On Big-Ticket Purchases
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: The festive season, usually a time to splurge, is telling a different story this year. A smaller number of card…
item.content:encoded:
The festive season, usually a time to splurge, is telling a different story this year. A smaller number of card transactions and weaker smartphone sales are hinting at consumers tightening their purse strings amid mounting pressure on household budgets.

Early data from Redseer estimated that India’s online festive sales clocked $7-8 Bn in gross merchandise value (GMV) during the first leg, from October 8 to 18. Nearly 100 Mn shoppers placed more than 350 Mn orders, with consumption running at around three times the everyday rate.

However, the data also pointed to a more cautious spending environment. According to Datum Intelligence, a market intelligence and consumer data analytics company, the online festive sales amounted to ₹29,800-₹30,900 Cr this year, down 7-10% from ₹33,200 Cr during the corresponding four-day period last year. Card spending, too, declined 12-15% YoY. 

The broader consumer picture was also subdued. LocalCircles’ ‘Mood for the Consumer 2026’ survey estimated that urban households would spend ₹1.97 Lakh Cr on festive discretionary purchases this year, down 6% from ₹2.10 Lakh Cr in 2025. The survey received more than 67,000 responses from urban consumers across 307 districts. 

The trends pointed to a central challenge for retailers: consumers continued to browse and buy, but rising expenses, uncertainty over earnings and jobs, and less compelling discounts made them more cautious about committing to expensive purchases. 

Shoppers Tune In But Spending Remains Muted

Flipkart’s ‘Big Billion Days’ sale, which opened on October 8 and closed on October 19, recorded 6.3 Mn concurrent users in a minute during its opening hour. 

Listed Meesho’s ‘Mega Blockbuster Sale’, which went live on October 9 and wrapped up on October 18, also reported a 75% YoY rise in day-one orders and 60% growth in transacting customers. 

Over at Amazon, the ecommerce major said that its nearly two-week long ‘Great Indian Festival’ sale (stretching between October 8 and October 20) saw the number of products ordered during the first twenty four hours more than double YoY.

Redseer’s assessment also highlighted the expanding reach of online festive shopping beyond major cities. Tier II and smaller towns accounted for around two-thirds of shoppers during the first leg, while the number of first-time shoppers from these regions doubled in 2026. 

Gen Z made up more than 35-40% of festive shoppers, with demand across gaming devices, creator cameras,wearables, sports footwear, grooming and beauty. 

Around 60% of Flipkart’s festive demand came from non-metro customers, while more than 72% of Amazon’s visits came from outside the top nine metros. Meesho also reported strong growth in orders through its Meesho Mall offering.

However, traffic, visitors and orders measured different aspects of shopping activity. They did not, by themselves, establish how much consumers spent or whether the average purchase value increased. 

Datum’s card payment data offered another view. On October 9, the first day Amazon and Flipkart opened their sales to all shoppers, card transactions stood at 83.5 Lakh against 82 Lakh on the corresponding day last year. Yet, the value of those payments fell 18% to ₹6,594 Cr from ₹8,067 Cr. 

The figures point to lower spending despite a similar number of card transactions. Meesho’s order growth, much of which came through cash on delivery, also illustrated why order counts alone could not establish the value of sales. 

The year-on-year comparison, however, comes with an important caveat. The major online sales in 2025 coincided with the September 22 GST rate cuts, which reduced prices on several consumer products. The opening of this year’s sales did not have a comparable tax-led trigger. 

Fashion And Select Categories Find Buyers

Category-level disclosures showed that consumers spent on fashion and certain premium products, even as electronics faced pressure.

A Bank of America research note (dated October 20) found that Myntra’s daily active users rose around 40% during the first six days of its ‘Big Fashion Festival’, which ran between October 8  and October 25, compared with its September average. 

Myntra’s monthly active users stood at around 93 Mn (up 8% YoY), while Nykaa Fashion’s monthly active users grew 24% to around 17 Mn.

Flipkart also reported a 42% YoY rise in beauty sales during the first hour of its sale, while its lifestyle category grew 12.5%, according to the company’s disclosures. Meesho also reported demand for festive décor and other lower-priced products.

Redseer’s category-level estimates showed that large and small appliances recorded more than 20 times their average daily GMV during the festive period. Electronics ran over seven times the everyday level, while mobiles exceeded five times. These multiple compared festive daily GMV with the January – August 2026 daily average, rather than with the previous year. 

Amazon’s disclosures show that some premium categories performed well. Televisions measuring 55 inches and above accounted for 65% of its TV sales, while premium Android smartphones’ sales rose 70% YoY. The company also reported that high-end home theatre sold at 100X its regular day levels, while front-load washing machines with capacities of 9 kg and above sold at 80X. 

Fashion and beauty also recorded strong festive demand. Redseer estimated that fashion grew 20-25% and accounted for nearly a fifth of festive GMV, making it the second largest category. 

However, these numbers reflected performance in specific categories and do not establish a broad recovery in big ticket demand. 

LocalCircles’ survey provided another indication of household priorities. Among respondents who planned festive discretionary spending, 72% intended to buy clothing, footwear or accessories. Home appliances and furniture and travel and holidays were each cited by 45%. Only 22% planned to buy mobile phones, consumer electronics or gadgets. 

The findings suggested that expensive electronics were not a priority for most households planning festive purchases. 

Household Budget Under Pressure

LocalCircles estimated that urban households would spend around ₹20,000 on festive discretionary purchases in 2026. While 57% of respondents said they intended to spend, 31% planned no discretionary festive purchases.

The survey’s findings on how households planned to fund their purchases were equally telling. Around 83% of households intending to spend expected to use savings to some extent. About 34% expected savings to cover at least a quarter of their festive expenditure, including 16% who said they would fund the entire amount from savings.

This came as retail inflation stood at 5.54% in September and food inflation at 7.74%, according to figures cited by LocalCircles. Higher everyday expenses left households with less room for purchases. 

LocalCircles founder Sachin Taparia said, “Household earnings are not rising, and inflation continues to rise.” He also pointed to concerns over AI and its potential effect on white-collar jobs, along with a lack of attractive deals on online commerce platforms. 

Discounts may also have done less to persuade shoppers to buy. The Economic Times reported that festive discounts were 35-40% lower than last year. The report also cited price increases of 30-40% for premium electronics in recent months. 

Smartphone Sales Exposed The Limits of Online Traffic

Smartphones provided one of the clearest indications of the pressure on high-value purchases. Counterpoint Research’s early assessment found that smartphone sales fell 16% YoY during the first three days of Amazon’s and Flipkart’s festive sales, despite strong traffic on both platforms.

The research firm had initially forecast a 12% decline in festive smartphone volumes. Its early assessment suggested that the fall could be steeper, although the figures available in the supporting documents did not establish the final full-season outcome. 

Counterpoint’s report identified higher device prices and fewer direct discounts as factors weighing on demand. Brands relied more on no-cost EMIs, bank cashback and exchange offers to make upgrades affordable without cutting listed prices sharply. 

Premium Samsung models, including the Galaxy S25 Ultra and the S25 FE, found buyers, but their performance did not prevent the overall decline in smartphone sales during the opening days. Entry-level devices faced greater pressure because even discounted models were generally more expensive than a year ago. 

“We had projected a 12% decline in smartphone sales, but based on the first wave of festive sales, we would not be surprised if the decline deepens to around 16%. Platforms have seen strong traffic, but conversions have been weak. Premium smartphones, however, continue to sell well, which could support revenue despite pressure on volumes,” Tarun Pathak, Research Director at Counterpoint Research. 

Counterpoint also noted that the opening days fell during Pitru Pakha, when some consumers in North India traditionally defer purchases. Navratri began on October 11, after the initial sales period, leaving the full festive effect on offline demand to pay out later. 

With the online sales campaigns now over, the early figures underline the difficulty retailers faced in converting strong digital engagement into higher-value purchases.

Overall, with household budgets under pressure, rising product prices and fewer compelling discounts, shoppers appear to be prioritising essentials and selective purchases over expensive upgrades this festive season.

item.content:encoded:
Update | October 23, 2026, 19:45 IST

Reliance Industries’ digital services arm Jio Platforms’ ₹30,213 Cr IPO was subscribed 22.19X on the third and final day of bidding, with investors bidding for 438.26 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data.

Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) led demand, subscribing their allotted portion 70.55X, with bids for 345.76 Cr shares against 4.90 Cr shares reserved for the category.

The non-institutional investor (NII) portion was subscribed 14X, receiving bids for 51.04 Cr shares against 3.64 Cr shares on offer.

Within the NII category, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 15.89X, while the segment for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 10.22X.

The retail investor portion was subscribed 2.72X, with bids for 23.12 Cr shares against 8.50 Cr shares on offer. The employee and shareholder portions were subscribed 2.93X and 7.60X, respectively.

Original | October 23, 2026, 12:14 IST

Reliance Industries’ digital services arm Jio Platforms’ IPO was subscribed 6.76X as of 11:48 IST on the third and final day of bidding, with institutional investors continuing to drive demand.

Investors bid for 133.51 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE subscription data. The overall subscription rose from 5.57X at the end of the second day.

Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) subscribed their allotted portion 14.18X, placing bids for 69.49 Cr shares against 4.90 Cr shares reserved for the category.

Within the institutional segment, domestic financial institutions, including banks and insurance companies, bid for 34.51 Cr shares, followed by foreign institutional investors at 26.19 Cr shares and mutual funds at 4.36 Cr shares.

The non-institutional investors’ (NIIs) portion was subscribed 9.17X, receiving bids for 33.44 Cr shares against an allocation of 3.64 Cr shares. Within this category, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 10.50X, while that for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was booked 6.52X.

Retail investors bid for 16.96 Cr shares against 8.50 Cr shares reserved, translating into 1.99X subscription. Meanwhile, the employee and shareholder portions were subscribed 2.46X and 5.59X, respectively.

Inside Jio’s Mega IPO

Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065–₹1,119 per share for the IPO, which opened on October 21 and closes today. At the upper end, the ₹30,213 Cr (about $3.2 Bn) offering surpasses Hyundai Motor India’s ₹27,870 Cr issue to become India’s largest IPO and values Jio Platforms at around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr (about $108 Bn).

Ahead of the public issue, Jio Platforms raised ₹8,109.8 Cr from anchor investors by allotting about 7.25 Cr shares at ₹1,119 apiece. Participants included HDFC Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, SBI Mutual Fund, BlackRock, the Government of Singapore, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.

The IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, with no offer-for-sale component. Jio plans to use ₹27,500 Cr to prepay certain borrowings of its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL), with the remaining proceeds earmarked for general corporate purposes.

The debt repayment makes the offering partly a balance sheet exercise, while its growth prospects depend on expanding beyond telecom connectivity into broadband, cloud services, enterprise solutions, and AI.

RJIL had 533.3 Mn customers as of June 30, 2026, while Jio’s network carried around 60% of India’s wireless data traffic in FY26. Jio Platforms’ operating revenue rose nearly 15% YoY to ₹1.47 Lakh Cr in FY26, while net profit increased 15.1% to ₹30,049 Cr.

item.title: Unicommerce Q2: Profit Rises 11% YoY To ₹6.4 Cr, Revenue Up 15%
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Ecommerce SaaS company Unicommerce reported a consolidated net profit of ₹6.4 Cr in the September quarter of FY27, up 11%…
item.content:encoded:
Ecommerce SaaS company Unicommerce reported a consolidated net profit of ₹6.4 Cr in the September quarter of FY27, up 11% from ₹5.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter.

On a sequential basis, net profit increased 37% from ₹4.7 Cr.

Operating revenue grew 15% YoY and QoQ to ₹59.1 Cr during the quarter. Including other income of ₹1.6 Cr, total income stood at ₹60.7 Cr, up 16% from ₹52.2 Cr a year earlier.

However, total expenses increased 19% YoY to ₹52.8 Cr, outpacing revenue growth. 

Net profit growth was supported by a decline in tax expense to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹2 Cr in Q2 FY26. This included a deferred tax credit of ₹1.4 Cr, compared with ₹8.5 Lakh a year earlier.

Its adjusted EBITDA for the quarter amounted to ₹10 Cr, indicating a 17% adjusted EBITDA margin. 

The company said that its profitability had been affected by planned investments in product development, talent, sales and marketing. It expects its profitability to increase in H2 FY27 as “incremental investments moderate”.

It added 121 enterprise clients including United Colors of Benetton, Macho, Furlenco, and others during the quarter. It also launched Uniware’s second-generation AI product, DNA, enabling customers to automate operational responses and make faster decisions. 

The company attributed its growth to continued momentum across its Uniware and Shipway businesses. Uniware, its ecommerce order management platform, recorded 14.5% YoY revenue growth, while Shipway grew 15.7%.

“Uniware’s growth trajectory continued to improve, supported by new enterprise additions and increasing adoption of newer modules. Shipway crossed the ₹100 crore annualised revenue run rate milestone, supported by independent customer acquisition and growing cross-sell synergies with Uniware. Our international business also continues to expand profitably,” CEO and MD Kapil Makhija said. 

For context, Unicommerce is owned by Snapdeal. It offers an ecommerce enablement SaaS platform which enables end-to-end management of ecommerce operations for brands, sellers and logistics service provider firms. 

Notably, Unicommerce and Snapdeal’s parent company AceVector recently debuted on the exchanges as well. It raised ₹420 Cr via its IPO, comprising a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS of up to 4.16 Cr shares, worth ₹133 Cr at the issue price. While the IPO saw 4.93X oversubscription, AceVector’s stock debuted at an 18.5% discount to the issue price and has seen a cold reception since, trending downwards. 

Shares of Unicommerce ended the day 4.58% lower at ₹76.09 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Zetwerk Makes Its Market Debut; Can Scale Alone Widen Its Thin Margins?
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Companies change course in good times and bad. For Zetwerk, the key turn came after it raised $150 Mn from…
item.content:encoded:
Companies change course in good times and bad. For Zetwerk, the key turn came after it raised $150 Mn from D1 Capital Part­ners in August 2021 when Indian startups raised a record $42 Bn in the calendar year.  

And what began as a platform to connect manufacturers to vendors and suppliers, turned into a full stack manufacturing play on the back of a bevy of acquisitions in 2021 and 2022. 

The company, founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan and Vishal Chaudhary, made its stock market debut today (Friday, October 23) with that full-stack promise at the centre of its pitch. No longer is this a marketplace, but a full-fledged platform that manages everything from procurement, supply, manufacturing, specifications and delivery. 

While the listing itself was not at a massive premium like some other new-age tech stocks, that’s besides the point when looking at the business model and the sector.  

The thesis around manufacturing remains strong for years to come as companies in key segments such as electric vehicles are looking to bring more of their component sourcing to India including in vital areas like precision machined parts. This was the opportunity that Zetwerk wanted to capture with its shift from marketplace to manufacturing. 

In FY26, its revenue from operations rose 40.4% YoY to ₹15,913 Cr, from ₹11,331 Cr in the previous fiscal. Yet, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606 Cr from ₹371 Cr in FY25. This loss includes an exceptional charge of ₹836 Cr from continuing operations and a ₹453 Cr impairment related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business.

Those are the realities of working in the manufacturing space. Opportunities come and go and companies have to react in terms of pivoting their operations. The impairment itself is not a major number, but what could worry investors is that adjusted EBITDA stood at a mere ₹421 Cr, translating into a margin of just 2.65% against the revenue. 

Plus, cash flows present another challenge. Zetwerk’s cash outflow from operations widened to ₹682 Cr in FY26 from ₹386 Cr a year earlier, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.4% to ₹12,370 Cr. 

A larger order book offers revenue visibility, but fulfilling those orders requires the company to fund procurement, production and logistics, while managing payments to suppliers and collections from customers. Let’s dive deeper into this as this is what investors will look at. 

The Two Revenue Pillars

Zetwerk operates through two main business segments: manufacturing and ecosystem. The latter operates under the Terra91 brand and supplies industrial raw materials such as steel, aluminium, copper, zinc, lead and bitumen.

The manufacturing business, which focuses on custom-made industrial products and related projects, is the largest of the two.

Together, the two businesses generated ₹15,913 Cr in revenue from continuing operations in FY26, up 40.4% YoY. Manufacturing accounted for ₹9,375 Cr, or 58.9% of revenue, while ecosystem contributed ₹6,539 Cr, or 41.1%. 

Simply put, the manufacturing business earns revenue by working with third-party manufacturers and Zetwerk’s own facilities to fulfil orders across energy products, precision machined products and capital goods. 

Its earnings depend on the price charged to customers relative to supplier payments, materials and fulfilment costs. More complex work, such as precision manufacturing requiring tight tolerances, can command a higher take rate than relatively less complex products. 

Notably, Zetwerk doesn’t disclose these margins and fees as it is likely to depend on the product and client needs, since this is how the industry functions.

In an earlier Inc42 interview, cofounder and CEO Acharya said the company does not consider commission when accounting for revenue. He described the model instead as a take rate for services. He said rates vary across product categories depending on the complexity of the work.

The manufacturing segment reported a standalone EBITDA of ₹565 Cr in FY26, translating into a margin of 6.03%. 

The other side is the ecosystem, which has grown considerably since 2022 as we indicated in the beginning. 

Unlike manufacturing, where Zetwerk coordinates production, the ecosystem segment aggregates demand for industrial raw materials, procures them in bulk and resells them to customers. 

Its economics are driven by the spread between procurement and selling prices, after accounting for logistics and other fulfillment costs. The segment’s Adjusted EBITDA stood at around ₹81 Cr, giving it a margin of approximately 1.24%.

The thin margin means that changes in commodity prices, sourcing costs or delivery expenses can have a significant impact on profitability, which we will see soon. Plus, the margin is considerably thinner than in manufacturing. 

These segment-level margins offer a view of Zetwerk’s economics, but the company has not disclosed commission rates or order-level profitability. 

Zetwerk’s revenue from operations includes the sale of products, income from construction and project contracts, sale of services and other operating revenue. 

Product sales cover manufactured goods, products sourced from third-party suppliers and industrial raw materials sold through the ecosystem business. Construction and project contract income relates to projects involving broader execution responsibilities, while service revenue includes activities such as job work and related services. 

Here’s the key difference from any other marketplace: Zetwerk acts as the principal in these transactions rather than simply connecting buyers and suppliers for a fee. It takes responsibility for sourcing, quality and delivery, meaning the revenue it reports reflects the value of goods and services sold, while procurement and fulfillment costs are recorded separately.

This is precisely the turn that Zetwerk’s 2021 fundraise and subsequent expansion allowed. 

Zetwerk’s Big Opportunity

Having said that, as we mentioned in the beginning, the problem for the company is that it operates with razor thin margins. Even as the adjusted EBITDA margin has improved year-on-year, it’s still not quite robust enough. 

Fulfilling industrial orders starts with a substantial procurement bill and procurement costs almost always escalate when there is a disparity in the order book. The key thing for Zetwerk will be to double down in one or two categories which will allow it to maximise the arbitrage revenue. 

Economies of scale will drive arbitrage revenue in the manufacturing business, especially when Zetwerk owns and controls the procurement side of the business. So manufacturing cannot drive profits on its own and Zetwerk will have to flesh out both sides of the business at the same time. 

Owning procurement removes third-party broker fees, distributor markups, and structural inefficiencies. The company captures the full margin that middle-men usually take. 

Add to that, sourcing inputs from low-cost regions which allows you to absorb fixed costs of logistics, customs, and compliance. 

And as the procurement side of the business scales up, Zetwerk will also have leverage for exclusive, long-term low-price contracts. 

But it’s not a flick of the switch, buying in extreme bulk can exponentially increase warehousing, insurance, and inventory carrying costs. Moreover, commodity price volatility is another factor since companies can get locked in to massive forward contracts even as market price shifts. So any arbitrage advantage gets flipped here. 

In FY26, the company spent ₹9,880 Cr on purchases of stock-in-trade and another ₹3,964 Cr on materials consumed, making these its two largest expense heads. Together, they accounted for nearly 86% of its total expenses of ₹16,142 Cr.

Purchases of stock-in-trade largely represent goods bought from suppliers and resold to customers. This expense head rose 45.3% YoY to ₹9,880 Cr in FY26 from ₹6,800 Cr in the previous fiscal. 

The cost of materials consumed includes materials used in manufacturing and project contracts — which increased 31% YoY to ₹3,964 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹3,036 Cr. The two expense heads reflect the procurement-heavy nature of Zetwerk’s business, where revenue growth requires the company to source goods, materials and manufacturing capacity to meet customer orders.

Why Revenue Growth Is Not Translating Into Cash

Zetwerk’s cash flow numbers point to the pressure of achieving the balance between procurement and manufacturing. In FY26, its net cash outflow from operating activities widened to ₹682 Cr from ₹386 Cr in FY25, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.3% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹12,370 Cr.

A growing order book provides visibility into future business, but it does not immediately translate into cash in the bank. Zetwerk still needs to source materials, pay suppliers and coordinate production to fulfil orders, while customer payments may come in only after goods are delivered or project milestones are met. 

This gap between spending on fulfillment and collecting revenue can tie up cash as the business expands.

The company’s procurement-heavy model means it’s particularly important that Zetwerk gets this balance right. As order volumes rise, the company may need to deploy more working capital to support the procurement, manufacturing and fulfillment needs, even if each order itself is profitable.

The challenge is therefore not simply to grow revenue or expand the order book, but to wring out inefficiencies in terms of arbitrage price, production bottlenecks and generally save costs through tech and AI.  

This will help the company mitigate the risks of delayed cash inflows and receivables. In FY26, Zetwerk’s trade receivables increased by ₹336 Cr, while its other financial and current assets rose by ₹715 Cr. 

Zetwerk’s ability to improve cash conversion will depend on how efficiently it manages inventory, supplier terms, production timelines, fulfillment and customer collections as it scales. Converting the order book pipeline into cash remains a big test of its business model.

Which is why Zetwerk is looking to capture more value by taking on design and engineering responsibilities, rather than simply manufacturing products to customer specifications. 

Its original design manufacturing (ODM) contracts accounted for 13.93% of manufacturing gross merchandise value (GMV) in FY26. Such work can offer better margins because it involves design and co-development, while also making customer relationships harder to replace.

Zetwerk is also trying to balance its supplier network with greater control over complex manufacturing. It operated 26 manufacturing facilities across four countries as of June 2026, while continuing to rely on third-party manufacturers for most of its manufacturing business.

Products sourced from third-party suppliers accounted for 80.46% of manufacturing segment revenue in FY26, down from 96.51% in FY24. This suggests that Zetwerk is gradually reducing its dependence on external capacity, but has not moved away from the model that helped it scale without investing in every stage of production.

But is scale alone enough to improve profitability? And now as a public company, Zetwerk will have to answer this tricky question.  

[Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam]

item.title: Netflix Credits Flipkart Bundle, Indian Shows For Record Q3 Subscriber Additions
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Streaming giant Netflix recorded its highest-ever quarterly paid net subscriber additions in India in the September quarter of 2026, crediting…
item.content:encoded:
Streaming giant Netflix recorded its highest-ever quarterly paid net subscriber additions in India in the September quarter of 2026, crediting a strong local content slate and its first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart.

Revenue in India grew about 18% YoY on a foreign exchange-neutral basis, which excludes the impact of currency movements, Netflix said in its quarterly shareholder letter. Viewing hours rose 24% YoY, while viewing hours per member increased by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage.

Netflix did not disclose the number of paid net additions in India or how many came through the Flipkart partnership.

During its Q3 earnings call, co-CEO Greg Peters pointed to India as an example of how locally produced titles were translating into higher engagement, membership growth, and revenue.

Local Content Drives Engagement

Lock Upp, Netflix’s first daily reality series, recorded more viewing hours in India than any other title on the platform, measured over its first 91 days.

The scripted series Musafir Cafe recorded 9 Mn views, while Operation Safed Sagar clocked 11 Mn views.

The India performance formed part of broader growth across Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Peters said local titles in these regions were driving engagement and business growth.

He also said Netflix’s subscriber retention remained healthy across regions. Globally and in the US, churn – the rate at which subscribers leave the service – improved YoY in Q3 and was lower than the company had forecast.

Globally, Netflix reported revenue of $12.87 Bn in Q3 2026, up 12% YoY. Operating income rose 37% to $4.46 Bn, while its operating margin expanded to 34.6% from 28.2% a year earlier.

For 2026, Netflix expects revenue of $51.1 Bn, representing 13% YoY growth.

Neumann said membership growth, pricing, and advertising were expected to support strong revenue growth in 2027, although the company had yet to issue formal guidance for the year.

Netflix also plans to introduce its advertising-supported subscription tier in 15 additional countries in 2027, with the first launches scheduled for March.
