item.title: Y Combinator-Backed Firstwork Nets $15 Mn To Expand Footprint Across US And Europe
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: US-based HR tech startup Firstwork has raised $15 Mn (over ₹142 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by…
item.content:encoded:
US-based HR tech startup Firstwork has raised $15 Mn (over ₹142 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Earlybird Venture Capital, as it looks to expand its AI-led workforce automation platform across the US and Europe.

The round also saw participation from Legion VC and Deel Ventures, along with existing investors Gradient and Y Combinator. The latest fundraise takes Firstwork’s total funding to $20 Mn since its launch in 2024.

The San Francisco-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand its teams across applied AI, AI research, engineering and go-to-market functions. Important to highlight that about 80% of the startup’s workforce operates from Bengaluru.

It also plans to deepen its presence in the US and Europe and extend its AI agents to more workforce operations.

Founded by ex-Deel executives Vardhan Kapoor and Shubham Choudhary, Firstwork uses AI agents to automate HR operations pertaining to frontline workers. These include document verification, background and right-to-work checks, onboarding, training coordination, compliance management and worker follow-ups.

The startup’s platform integrates within existing HR systems, allowing employers to automate workflows without replacing their existing software.

According to Firstwork, more than 1.50 Lakh frontline workers start work through its platform every month. It claims that its platform has helped these customers cut the time spent by workers and HR teams on each new hire by up to 90%. Its clientele features the likes of Deel, Job&Talent, Relay, Wonolo and BGSF. 

AI is seeing a broad band adoption in the human resource function and is rechanging the face of enterprise tech globally. While Firstwork is primarily targeting the global market, the Indian is projected to double in value to $2.3 Bn by 2033 from $1.12 Bn in 2024.

Leveraging AI, several Indian startups are building solutions to capture this booming market. For instance, Bengaluru-based Hunar.AI, which raised ₹40 Cr earlier this week, is using conversational AI agents to automate gig-worker hiring, onboarding, training and employee retention. Its clients include Swiggy, Zepto, Croma, Starbucks and Dr Lal PathLabs.

Hyderabad-based TurboHire also raised $6 Mn in a Series A round led by IvyCap Ventures in August 2025 to scale its agentic AI-based recruitment platform. Founded in 2019, the startup automates enterprise hiring workflows and claims to have onboarded more than 120 enterprises, including Cipla, Tata Motors, PwC, Lenskart and Britannia.

Other players operating in adjacent segments include TraqCheck, which offers AI-powered background verification and recruitment agents, and HireBound, which automates candidate sourcing, screening and evaluation, competes with Firstwork

item.content:encoded:
Update | October 23, 2026, 16:40 IST

Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging’s shares closed their debut session at ₹1,133.65 on the BSE, 61.95% above their issue price of ₹700 but 2.44% below their listing price of ₹1,162.

On the NSE, the stock closed at ₹1,133.80, a 61.97% premium to its issue price and 2.26% below its listing price of ₹1,160.

During the session, shares touched highs of ₹1,209.85 on the BSE and ₹1,211 on the NSE, representing gains of 72.84% and 73%, respectively, over the issue price.

At the BSE closing price, Tonbo Imaging’s market capitalisation stood at ₹6,493.79 Cr ($684.1 Mn).

Original | October 23, 2026, 10:00 IST

Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging made a strong stock market debut, listing at ₹1,162 on the BSE, a 66% premium to its issue price of ₹700 per share.

On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹1,160, translating into a listing gain of 65.71%. The company commanded a market capitalisation of ₹6,656.18 Cr (about $701.3 Mn) on the BSE at its listing price.

The debut followed strong investor demand for Tonbo’s ₹852 Cr IPO, which was open for subscription from October 15 to October 19 at a price band of ₹665-₹700 per share.

The public issue was subscribed 135.9X, attracting bids for 115.87 Cr shares against the 85.26 Lakh shares on offer.

The IPO comprised entirely an offer for sale (OFS) of around 1.22 Cr shares by existing shareholders, with no fresh issue component. Consequently, Tonbo will receive no proceeds from the public offering.

Tonbo’s cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza collectively pocketed ₹137.2 Cr by selling shares through the IPO, with Lakshmikumar accounting for ₹80.5 Cr of the proceeds.

Ahead of the bidding, the company secured ₹255.4 Cr from anchor investors, allotting 36.5 Lakh shares to 43 investors at ₹700 apiece. Participants included SBI Mutual Fund, Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and WhiteOak Capital.

Inside Tonbo’s Defence Business

Tonbo was bought out from Sarnoff Corporation in 2012 by promoters and cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza. It subsequently pivoted from research and technology development services to designing advanced imaging and sensor systems for military applications.

Its portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, fire-control systems, and missile seekers used for surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting. The startup handles prototype development, system integration, and qualification testing in-house, while outsourcing manufacturing to partners including Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology.

The strong listing comes despite a decline in Tonbo’s FY26 financial performance. Operating revenue fell 22.7% YoY to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹469.1 Cr, while net profit declined about 30% to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr.

In Q1 FY27, the startup reported a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr on operating revenue of ₹36 Cr.

Speaking to Inc42, CEO Lakshmikumar attributed the FY26 revenue decline to delays in executing international programmes, which pushed deliveries into FY27.

item.title: The CFO Code: Perfios’ Prashant Mahagaonkar On Balancing Founder Ambition With Financial Discipline
item.dc:creator: Anirudh Trivedi
item.description: Getting an acquisition across the finish line can take months of negotiations, due diligence, paperwork and financial scrutiny. But closing…
item.content:encoded:
Getting an acquisition across the finish line can take months of negotiations, due diligence, paperwork and financial scrutiny. But closing the deal is only half the battle. The real challenge comes when you integrate the business, unlock synergies, and deliver the value that justified the deal in the first place.

Much of this heavy lifting falls on CFOs, who are expected to go beyond balancing the books to evaluate acquisition targets, assess financial risks, structure deals and ensure the business derives long-term value from the transaction.

This is part of a broader shift in the CFO’s role, from financial oversight to strategic decision-making. Whether determining how to extract value from an acquisition or assessing if an investment in AI will deliver adequate returns, finance leaders are making critical capital-allocation decisions while ensuring the business stays on track to meet its growth ambitions.

At Perfios, a B2B SaaS fintech serving more than 1,000 financial institutions across multiple geographies, Group CFO Prashant Mahagaonkar sits at the heart of these decisions. 

With more than 25 years of experience across traditional finance, multinational companies, M&A and venture-backed businesses, Mahagaonkar’s career has given him a front-row seat to the changing nature of the finance function. 

For the concluding edition of The CFO Code series, Inc42 caught up with Mahagaonkar to discuss his experiences and learnings from decades of building finance systems, integrating acquisitions and working alongside founders and CEOs.

Speaking with Inc42, Mahagaonkar broke down how his role has evolved, what he has learnt from acquisitions, why CFOs need to question technology spending, and what he believes will define the next generation of finance leaders.

Walking The Tightrope Between Risk and Reward

Mahagaonkar’s career began in 1999 at Tata Motors, but he soon realised traditional audit and compliance work wasn’t where he wanted to build his career.

In 2022, Mahagaonkar joined Givaudan India, a Swiss flavour and fragrance major where he got his first real exposure to what a well-built financial system looked like. For Mahagaonkar, the experience became an education in how large organisations build systems and roll them out across markets.

Mahagaonkar then shifted to Essilor India, a spectacle lens manufacturing company, where he was exposed to acquisitions and moved from traditional finance to a more M&A- and business-oriented role. 

He later joined venture-backed Amba Research, where he raised capital, worked with investors across geographies and eventually managed an exit. Moody’s acquired the company. Mahagaonkar moved to CitiusTech, where he became the company’s first CFO and worked closely with the founder-CEO to scale revenue from roughly $60 Mn to $500 Mn. 

“Working with the founders to scale the team was a great learning experience for me. I realised how different a founder’s mindset is from that of a professional CEO. Their risk-taking appetite is very different, and they bring perspectives that a traditional professional may find difficult to act on,” said Mahagaonkar. 

As Mahagaonkar puts it, the experience taught him how to keep the company business-friendly while also protecting it financially. According to him, while founders may be willing to offer more flexibility to win a customer, the finance leader’s job is to ensure the company is adequately protected. 

“But the solution was not always to take the most conservative position. Instead, the finance team had to establish a playbook that clearly defined what it would agree to and where it would draw the line,” said Mahagaonkar. 

He added that finding “the art of the possible” within an accepted compliance framework is one of the most important skills he has developed over time.

Making Acquisitions Work Beyond The Deal

Mahagaonkar’s M&A experience proved valuable when he joined Perfios in July 2025. By then, the company had completed three acquisitions, and his mandate was to integrate the acquired businesses into a cohesive organisation.

Perfios acquired an eFRM (Enterprise Fraud Risk Management) business, a segment it had not historically operated in. In another acquisition, it added a collections company, adjacent to its existing loan origination, approval, and credit underwriting businesses. Each acquisition required a different integration strategy.

Mahagaonkar shared that his task was to determine what should be fully integrated into Perfios, what should retain its independence and how each business could contribute to the broader ecosystem. All this had to be done while ensuring that every entity remained compliant with the applicable regulatory and reporting requirements.

Smaller companies often lack the same level of compliance infrastructure as a private equity-backed or larger organisation. “Therefore, the integration process involved bringing acquired businesses up to Perfios’ standards across areas such as information security, contracts, insurance, risk and statutory compliance,” the CFO said.

However, amid all the finance and integration of compliance functions, what generally gets understated and undermined is the integration of people and cultures. 

Mahagaonkar argues that people integration is also a finance responsibility because acquisitions can easily leave redundant roles and overlapping functions in place.

“You need to put it together and be part of those discussions to help and make sure that we build that one organisation which is required,” he said.

AI Spend Under CFO’s Scanner

The expanding role of the CFO is particularly evident in capital allocation, where Mahagaonkar believes AI has fundamentally changed how technology investments are evaluated and prioritised.

“Today, product life cycles have shortened so much that companies may have just six months, rather than two years, to get ahead of competitors before they develop similar products,” he said.

For the CFO, this means asking harder questions about whether the company is deploying its capital into the right assets and whether its innovation engine is moving quickly enough to match the pace of competitors. 

But in this chase, increasing AI spend may seem like the obvious choice for almost every problem, and Mahagaonkar believes companies need to look before they leap. 

“Not every problem needs AI, particularly when a simple automation can do the job,” Mahagaonkar said.

At Perfios, the company has built an ROI matrix around its usage that monitors productivity gains, potential changes in hiring requirements and whether a particular use case should use AI at all, instead of automation or machine learning. 

Becoming The CEO’s Co-Pilot

With the changing relationship between finance and technology, Mahagaonkar believes the CFO has moved from being a backroom player to becoming a co-pilot to the CEO or founder. He also mentioned that being a co-pilot to the CEO does not mean becoming the de facto CEO.

Mahagaonkar estimates that around 40% of a CFO’s decisions today require forward-looking judgement rather than relying solely on historical financial data. 

When asked about the skill sets that will matter most for the next generation of CFOs, he said, “We must accept that today’s young people often know more than we do. They have greater access to information, and they can process and apply it much faster. The real test for the next generation of leaders, not just CFOs, will be managing such high-calibre talent, helping them find meaning in their work and creating an environment where they can succeed.”

According to Mahagaonkar, finance leaders of the past could succeed by knowing the numbers better than everyone else, but CFOs of the future will have to understand the numbers, the business, the technology and, increasingly, the people behind the decisions.

[Edited By Shishir Parasher]

item.title: Ola Electric Slides Over 7% After Bearish Call From Goldman Sachs
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Update | October 23, 16:55 IST Shares of Ola Electric ended the day 6.39% lower at ₹29.90 apiece on the…
item.content:encoded:
Update | October 23, 16:55 IST

Shares of Ola Electric ended the day 6.39% lower at ₹29.90 apiece on the BSE today, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,946.06 Cr ($1.58 Bn). The company’s shares are now trading 61% below its listing price of ₹76. 

Original | October 23, 14:31 IST

Shares of electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric crashed as much as 7.6% to hit an intraday low about ₹29 on the BSE today (October 23) after a bearish outlook from Goldman Sachs. 

A day after the company opened its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, Goldman Sachs downgraded its outlook on Ola Electric to “Sell”. The brokerage slashed the stock’s price target to ₹23.

It foresees a challenging path for Ola Electric to become cash flow positive given the relatively high interest cost and capex needs of the cell and E2W business.

It also cut the EV maker’s top line growth projections by up to 10% for the period FY27-29.

The bearish momentum comes a day after Ola Electric opened its rights issue for bidding. Within hours of opening the issue, Motilal Oswal and Calliope Capital Advisors applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by two promoter group entities — ANI Technologies and Indus Trust. 

Founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the company’s proposed rights issue of up to ₹1,000 Cr.

Ola Electric plans to use the proceeds from its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue primarily to reduce debt and fund business expansion as it looks to strengthen its financial position and move towards cash-flow breakeven. 

Of the total proceeds, ₹350 Cr has been earmarked for the repayment or prepayment of borrowings, including accrued interest and applicable penalties, while ₹400 Cr will be invested in organic growth across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses. 

Ola Electric is yet to report its second quarter earnings results. As of Q1 FY27, the company trimmed its net loss by 22% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue declined 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26. 

As of 13:52 IST, the stock was down 6.57% at ₹29.87 per share on the BSE, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,931.06 Cr ($1.57 Bn).

If losses hold, this would be the sixth straight session of the stock ending in red. In the past one month, the stock has lost over 20% in value.

item.title: IPO-Bound Garuda Aerospace’s FY26 Profit Jumps 41% To ₹25.9 Cr
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Chennai-based dronetech startup Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹25.9 Cr in FY26, growing 41.1% from ₹18.4 Cr from…
item.content:encoded:
Chennai-based dronetech startup Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹25.9 Cr in FY26, growing 41.1% from ₹18.4 Cr from the previous fiscal year. 

In terms of operational profitability, the drone maker’s EBITA for the fiscal year jumped 31.8% to ₹35.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹26.6 Cr in the FY25. 

Operating revenue surged 66.8% YoY to ₹206 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹123.5 Cr in the previous year. Sales of drones and drone parts brought in ₹99.4 Cr to the top line while the remaining ₹106.5 Cr via sale of services. Another ₹15 Lakh was earned from delivery charges. 

Including other income of ₹26.5 Lakh, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹206.2 Cr.

“During the year, we continued to strengthen our manufacturing capabilities, expand our Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) operations, deepen our investment in indigenous research and development, and build strategic partnerships in India and international markets. We also advanced our capabilities in artificial intelligence, autonomous flight, data analytics, defence systems and specialised mission platforms,” cofounder and whole-time director Agnishwar Jayaprakash noted in a message to shareholders. 

The improvement in the financial performance comes as Garuda’s proposed public listing plans take shape. The startup took the pre-filing route to confidentially submit its draft IPO papers with the SEBI earlier in April. The IPO was greenlit by the markets regulator in August. 

While the startup is yet to file its updated DRHP for public access, its board approved plans to raise up to ₹750 Cr via the fresh issue component of the proposed IPO back in March. As per reports, the OFS component could result in investors offloading shares worth as much as ₹250 Cr.

In its annual report for FY26, the startup disclosed that its board of directors had approved a  private placement of equity shares worth ₹57.2 Cr back in August. Investors who backed the startup were Umasankar Nistala, Rakesh Pillai, Jitendra Rana, Vimaan Innovators LLP and Aditum Management.

The proceeds of the issue would fuel business growth, working capital requirements, and be used for loan repayments. 

The startup claims to have become India’s largest drone maker, having manufactured and sold over 3000 drones. It also claimed to be the first drone company to partner with three defence PSUs. 

It has raised a total funding of over $37 Mn to date from investors like Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle, cricketer Mahendra Singh Dhoni, among others. It was last valued at $250 Mn after raising a $11 Mn Series B funding round led by Venture Catalysts. 

Where Did Garuda Aerospace Spend In FY26?

Garuda Aerospace’s total expenses in FY26 rose 73.2% YoY to ₹172.2 Cr from ₹99.4 Cr in FY25.  It reported no exceptional items during the fiscal but bore ₹8.2 Cr tax expenses.

Here are the main operational expenses of the startup:

  • Cost of Materials Consumed: Representing the largest operational expense, raw material costs surged 61.5% YoY to ₹116.8 Cr from ₹72.3 Cr in FY25.
  • Impairment Losses on Financial Assets: Impairment losses amounted to ₹11.1 Cr in FY26, compared to ₹6.5 Lakh in the year-ago period. 
  • Employee Benefit Expenses: Garuda Aerospace’s personnel-related costs decreased 16.7% YoY to ₹8 Cr in FY26 from ₹9.6 Cr in the previous year. 
  • Depreciation And Amortisation Expenses: The cost recorded under this line item increased 13.3% YoY to ₹4.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹3.6 Cr in FY25. 
  • Other Expenses: Spending on items like professional expenses, travel, maintenance, rent, and other corporate overheads stayed nearly flat at ₹29.2 Cr.

item.title: WhatsApp, Telegram SIM-Binding Mandate To Take Effect From January 1: Report
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Messaging platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram are reportedly set to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ (DoT) SIM-binding mandate from January…
item.content:encoded:
Messaging platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram are reportedly set to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ (DoT) SIM-binding mandate from January 1, 2027, requiring their services to remain linked to the active SIM associated with a user’s registered mobile number.

According to a Times of India report, platforms must complete implementation by December 31, 2026, ahead of the reported operational start date the following day. The requirement could affect users who access messaging apps on phones without the associated SIM.

The mandate stems from directions issued by the DoT in November last year under the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024. The original directions named WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat, Arattai, ShareChat, Josh, and JioChat.

The department said some app-based communication services continued to function without the SIM associated with the registered mobile number being present in the device. According to the DoT, this allowed fraudsters operating from outside India to misuse Indian mobile numbers.

SIM binding requires covered services to remain continuously linked to the associated active SIM, rather than relying solely on verification when an account is first set up. The government said the measure was intended to improve traceability and curb phishing, digital arrest, impersonation, and investment scams.

The original directions gave platforms 90 days to implement the measures and 120 days to submit compliance reports. However, the government subsequently specified December 31, 2026, as the compliance deadline for SIM binding.

Platforms Prepare For Compliance

According to a CNBC report, Apple has updated its iOS software to support the SIM-binding requirements ahead of the implementation deadline.

WhatsApp and Arattai have confirmed that they are working to comply with the rules. Telegram is yet to clarify on its compliance status, while Signal has not responded to government notices, CNBC reported.

Snapchat has reportedly maintained that the mandate does not apply to its service because it does not use phone numbers to identify users.

Questions also remain about how individual platforms will support eSIM users. CNBC reported that WhatsApp and Telegram would require a physical SIM card to function, although the precise requirements for eSIM users have not been clarified.

The mandate could affect users who access messaging apps over Wi-Fi on phones without their registered SIM, as well as those who frequently switch SIMs. Its impact on access across multiple devices will depend on individual platforms’ implementation.

However, the DoT has clarified that international roaming will not be affected as long as the associated SIM remains in the handset.

The implementation push comes amid concerns over cyber fraud in India. According to data sourced from the home ministry, Indians lost ₹22,495 Cr to cyber fraud in 2025 compared with ₹22,845 Cr in 2024.

In June, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) said Indians had lost around ₹52,976 Cr to cyber-enabled fraud over the past six years, with nearly 8% of the losses linked to digital arrest scams.

Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi called on global technology companies, financial institutions, and telecom operators to work together to build a comprehensive framework to tackle cyber fraud and deepfakes.

“At a time when telecom and digital technology have become so important, it is equally important to make the security framework associated with it ironclad. It is our priority to secure mobile phones and networks,” Modi said, adding that trust was crucial for people using phones to communicate and make payments.

item.title: Ultraviolette Launches New E-Bike X-47 Venom With A ₹2.65 Lakh Price Tag
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: A month after raising $85 Mn, e-bike maker Ultraviolette has unveiled its new motorcycle, X-47 Venom powered by its new…
item.content:encoded:
A month after raising $85 Mn, e-bike maker Ultraviolette has unveiled its new motorcycle, X-47 Venom powered by its new VX-100 100V platform.

The motorcycle has been launched at an introductory price of ₹2.65 Lakh, applicable to the first 5,000 customers. Bookings opened on October 22. Deliveries are expected to commence in November 2026, the startup said in a press release.

The X-47 Venom is the first motorcycle built on Ultraviolette’s new VX-100 architecture. It combines the platform with its new UV LIGHTFURY electric motor and SRB-11 battery technology. It has peak power of 30 kW (39 bhp) and a 550 Nm of wheel torque. The Ultraviolette X-47 Venom is built to have a top speed of 155 kmph.

The motorcycle offers a claimed Indian Driving Cycle (IDC) range of 343 km. It can accelerate from 0 to 100 kmph in 5.9 seconds and has a kerb weight of 180 kg, making it up to 20 kg lighter than the previous-generation platform.

Ultraviolette Introduces New VX-100 Platform

The VX-100 is a new electrical architecture designed to improve energy efficiency, thermal management and charging speeds across Ultraviolette’s product portfolio.

The platform incorporates SRB-11 battery technology, which the startup claims offers up to 20% higher energy density and twice the cooling performance. Its thermal management system is designed to dissipate heat up to 50% faster, while the battery pack features a cast-aluminium housing and IP67 protection against dust and water ingress.

The motorcycle also features a new motor control unit that is twice as compact and delivers three times the power density, according to the company.

“The X-47 Venom reflects our approach to engineering the entire motorcycle as one integrated system,” Ultraviolette cofounder and CTO Niraj Rajmohan said.

He added that the modular architecture would allow the company to extend these technologies across future products as it expands its portfolio and global presence.

The bike adds to Ultraviolette’s portfolio of high-end, speed focused EV bikes. Ultraviolette’s flagship electric motorcycle lineup is currently anchored by the Ultraviolette F77 MACH 2 and F77 SuperStreet series. 

The startup is eyeing entry into the EV scooter segment soon, with production of e-scooter Tesseract as well as e-bike Shockwave expected to commence over the next few months.

Recently, the electric two-wheeler startup raised $85 Mn (about ₹813 Cr) in a Series E round co-led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures, to expand its manufacturing capacity and product portfolio, as well as strengthen its distribution network in India and overseas.

The startup is bolstering its manufacturing capabilities and plans to invest more than ₹1,000 Cr over the next five years to expand its manufacturing footprint. Its upcoming BIGGA Factory is set to take its annual production capacity to as much as 2.5 Lakh vehicles in the initial phase.

Ultraviolette currently has an installed capacity of around 30,000 vehicles annually at its Bengaluru facility, which is being expanded to 50,000-60,000 units. The plant will continue to serve as a manufacturing, engineering and technology hub after the BIGGA Factory comes online.

It is also targeting international markets, with exports expected to account for around 25% of revenue over the next five years.

item.title: CoinDCX Admits Losses From Old Wallet Deposits, Denies Breach Of Active Wallets
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Crypto exchange CoinDCX has acknowledged operational losses after a process meant to secure deposits sent to old, compromised wallet addresses…
item.content:encoded:
Crypto exchange CoinDCX has acknowledged operational losses after a process meant to secure deposits sent to old, compromised wallet addresses failed, while denying a breach of its active wallets.

In a post on X, the exchange said some users continued depositing crypto into addresses compromised during the July 2025 security incident, despite notifications asking them to use updated addresses available on its app and website.

CoinDCX said it regularly “sweeps” deposits sent to these discontinued addresses, moving the funds so they can be accounted for and secured. However, this process failed for a period, with the failure identified on the morning of its update.

“This failure led to some operational losses, which were absorbed by CoinDCX,” the exchange said.

The company did not disclose the amount lost or how long the process had failed. It said all affected users’ crypto deposits had been credited, including those sent to the discontinued addresses.

CoinDCX maintained that customer assets remained in segregated cold wallets and that its current central and user wallet addresses were unaffected. It also said no funds from active wallets had been compromised and that trading continued as usual.

Denial Followed By Disclosure

The update followed an earlier statement in which CoinDCX described claims circulating on X about certain wallet addresses and transactions as misleading.

Among these was a post by blockchain investigator Darcy, who flagged transfers of around $16 Mn worth of cryptocurrency from wallets linked to CoinDCX to another wallet.

According to the investigator, the funds were subsequently split across multiple addresses and routed to deposit addresses on exchanges including Binance, OKX, and Gate. CoinDCX has not confirmed whether these amounts correspond to the operational losses it disclosed.

In its initial response, the exchange said the flagged addresses had been created in January 2025, compromised during the July 2025 hack, and had not been used by CoinDCX since.

Cofounder and CEO Sumit Gupta separately denied a fresh wallet breach, saying hackers appeared to be reusing the compromised addresses.

Gupta said the exchange had checked its current central and user wallet addresses and found that none had transferred funds to the old addresses in question. He added that the team was investigating further.

The subsequent company update acknowledged that users had continued sending deposits to the discontinued addresses and that its process for securing those deposits had failed.

CoinDCX had lost around $44 Mn in a cyberattack in July 2025, when an internal operational account used to provide liquidity on a partner exchange was compromised.

At the time, the exchange said the stolen assets belonged to its treasury, customer funds were unaffected, and it would absorb the losses. It subsequently launched a recovery bounty programme to help trace and recover the stolen assets.

item.title: From Three Products To 450 SKUs: How R for Rabbit Built A ₹250 Cr Baby Care Brand Around Parents’ Concerns
item.dc:creator: Inc42 BrandLabs
item.description: India’s baby care market is growing, and so is the challenge of finding products parents can genuinely trust. When it…
item.content:encoded:
India’s baby care market is growing, and so is the challenge of finding products parents can genuinely trust. When it comes to baby care, Indian parents often look for the same thing: products that are made well, priced for the value they deliver, and worth bringing home. 

Ahmedabad-based Kunal and Kinjal Popat found themselves at the centre of this dilemma when they became parents in 2011. The couple began searching for a safer alternative, but that search opened another can of worms: finding a product that was safe, well-designed and priced right. 

Their hunt for safer alternatives soon hit a snag. While there was no shortage of baby products in the market, very few offered the combination of safety, thoughtful design and transparent pricing the couple was looking for.

Instead of compromising, the Popats decided to build what they could not find. Kunal brought over a decade of experience across engineering, marketing and sales, while Kinjal, trained in design, brought a different lens to the problem. Together, they set out to make baby products that put safety first with the right price tag. And that is how R for Rabbit came into being in 2014. 

The couple started with around ₹40 Lakh of their own savings, designing products in-house and working with established, safety-certified manufacturers. 

“I used to visit factories before finalising any partnerships to ensure quality control, testing and certification standards remain as we want for the brand,” said Kinjal.

Initially, R for Rabbit started with three baby-gear products, led by strollers. From there, the company began expanding its portfolio and distribution. Today, the brand controls more than 450 SKUs across categories such as car seats, baby apparel, personal care, feeding ranges, and ride-on toys. 

R for Rabbit expanded into kids’ personal care by launching the Biomimic baby skin care range in August this year and entered the baby clothing segment with its apparel range in September.

As it continues to grow its product portfolio and distribution, getting products to customers efficiently became an increasingly important part of its growth strategy. The company’s partnership with Shadowfax in 2026 reflects this shift, with last-mile delivery becoming a key consideration as the brand scales across markets.

Building A Full-Stack Baby Care Brand

At the outset, R for Rabbit relied heavily on word of mouth to build trust. Mothers who discovered the brand began recommending its products through WhatsApp groups and personal networks because of the brand’s focus on quality and international standards of safety.

This grassroots buzz helped the duo build early sales without leaning heavily on traditional advertising. Thanks to this organic growth, the brand’s portfolio grew to around 25 products by 2016.

“Over time, as our range grew, we put a much clearer framework around how we developed our products. We built everything around four pillars: safety, quality, innovation and customer support. For us, the highest quality and international standards are the floor, rather than the ceiling,” Kunal told Inc42. 

The founders’ focus was clear: the brand’s products should be designed around everyday realities of Indian parents. Strollers, for instance, were designed to fold with one hand, making them easier to manoeuvre in India’s often cramped lifts and busy urban spaces. Similarly, the founders focused on plug-and-play assemblies for parents to set up products without a complicated installation process. They also designed convertible high chairs that could double up as toddler desks. 

R for Rabbit also began developing and patenting more of its own products instead of selling products already available in the market. This helped the brand carve out a space between expensive imported brands and cheaper local alternatives. 

By 2019, R for Rabbit built a base of nearly 1.5 Mn parents. 

From Growth To A More Complex Fulfilment Model

The key change for R for Rabbit came when it moved beyond products that parents bought only occasionally. It entered toys with ‘Orapple Toys’ in 2020 and then launched Feather Diapers in 2022. 

The expansion into new categories also began to show up in R for Rabbit’s business numbers.

The company raised its first institutional round in October 2021, and by FY23, its revenue reached ₹128 Cr. It crossed ₹250 Cr in FY25, helped by a wider product portfolio that grew by more than 100 products during this period. 

Diapers, in particular, emerged as one of the company’s fastest-growing categories, giving the business a more consistent revenue stream.

The 2025-26 phase brought further expansion. In August 2025, R for Rabbit raised $27 Mn in Series B funding, led by Filter Capital and 3one4 Capital. In the following year, the company added BioMimic, a biomimicry-based kids’ personal care range, and launched its first apparel line.

In 2026, R for Rabbit’s offline reach crossed 3,000 retail touchpoints, while quick commerce emerged as another important channel. As the company added more products, repeat purchases and customers across more markets, fulfilment became a bigger part of the equation.

The challenge was no longer just having the right products, but getting them to customers quickly while keeping delivery costs in check. This also meant rethinking how it stored and moved inventory. 

R for Rabbit eventually moved from a single warehouse to a regional third-party logistics model, bringing inventory closer to customers across different markets. The company partnered with Shadowfax in 2026 to strengthen its last-mile network and offer same-day and next-day deliveries.

The primary aim of the partnership was to improve delivery speed and coverage as the brand continues to grow across categories and markets.

“We wanted to build a logistics network that could keep pace with our growth and get products to customers faster. As we expand across categories and markets, being closer to the customer becomes increasingly important. Our partnership with Shadowfax helps us strengthen that last-mile capability and improve both delivery speed and coverage,” says Kunal.

Shadowfax’s same-day and next-day delivery capabilities have helped the brand reach more pincodes and improve delivery timelines. According to Kunal, the partnership has brought tangible improvement in its turnaround times and greater operational flexibility.

As volumes increase, the company expects better logistics efficiency and wider coverage to help it grow revenue while keeping fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies under control. Faster delivery and broader coverage could also help reduce delivery-related drop-offs and improve the customer experience.

Scaling The Next Mile

For R for Rabbit, the next stage of growth will extend beyond its existing footprint. The company is looking to deepen its presence in Tier II, Tier III and other emerging markets while continuing to grow in metros.

This expansion will bring more customers, higher order volumes and greater demand for faster deliveries, making fulfilment an increasingly important part of the customer experience.

“As we work towards becoming a ₹1,000 Cr business, we know that our ability to serve customers across more locations will be critical. Partnering with Shadowfax lets us hold that promise on delivery too, with faster, more reliable fulfilment as we reach deeper into Tier II and Tier III India,” said Kunal.

That makes logistics more than just an operational function. Faster same-day and next-day deliveries can improve the customer experience, while better reverse logistics can make returns and exchanges easier. 

R for Rabbit maintains an overall NPS of 80+, reflecting the word-of-mouth loyalty that has helped build the brand. As the company expands, maintaining that trust will depend on delivering a consistent experience beyond the product itself.

By partnering with Shadowfax, R for Rabbit is strengthening its last-mile capabilities to support faster deliveries and wider coverage as it expands into new markets.

At the same time, expanding into new markets means R for Rabbit needs to bring inventory closer to customers without allowing fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies to rise.

From three baby-gear products in 2014 to a portfolio spanning everyday parenting needs, R for Rabbit has come a long way. But as the company enters its next phase, the challenge now is to make sure that its products reach customers quickly, reliably and efficiently.

Update| October 23, 2026, 16:32 IST

Shares of Swiggy ended today trading session 16.3% lower at ₹176.70 apiece on the BSE. Its market capitalisation stood at ₹48,774.7 Cr (about $5.1 Bn).

Notably, shares of the foodtech major have slipped 54.69% below their IPO price of ₹390. The stock listed on the exchanges in November 2024.

Original| October 23, 2026 11:52 IST

Foodtech major Swiggy’s shares plunged as much as 17.23% to a 52-week low of ₹174.90 on the BSE today, a day after its Q2 FY27 results showed widening losses at quick commerce arm Instamart.

The stock pared some losses to trade at ₹181.50, down 14.10%, at 11:21 IST. Its market capitalisation stood at ₹50,099.69 Cr (about $5.2 Bn) at that time.

Several brokerages lowered their price targets following the results, citing higher-than-expected quick commerce losses and concerns over Instamart’s growth and execution. However, most retained their existing ratings.

Swiggy’s consolidated net loss narrowed 16% YoY to ₹922 Cr in Q2 FY27 but widened 17% from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue rose 36% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr.

Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss increased to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier and ₹778 Cr in Q1 FY27, offsetting an improvement in food delivery profitability.

Brokerages Lower Price Targets 

Citi retained its ‘Buy’ rating but cut its target price to ₹330. It highlighted 18% YoY growth in food delivery gross order value (GOV), alongside margin improvements of 60 basis points YoY and 30 basis points QoQ. However, Instamart’s net order value (NOV) grew around 13% sequentially, below its estimate of 16%, while losses exceeded expectations.

CLSA retained its ‘Outperform’ rating but lowered its target price to ₹262. It said Instamart’s 13.4% sequential NOV growth fell short of expectations, while losses were higher than anticipated. The brokerage flagged a widening gap between Swiggy and Eternal in growth and profitability, adding that Instamart needs to deliver consistent improvements to rebuild investor confidence.

Nomura retained its ‘Buy’ rating but cut its target price to ₹300. It expects Swiggy’s food delivery business to generate ₹1,300 Cr to ₹1,900 Cr in EBITDA across FY27 and FY28. However, it said quick commerce execution continued to disappoint. The brokerage values food delivery at 40 times its estimated FY28 EBITDA and assigns no value to quick commerce or Swiggy’s cash balances.

Jefferies retained its ‘Buy’ rating but lowered its target price to ₹330. While food delivery revenue and EBITDA met expectations, it said reducing quick commerce losses remains critical.

UBS maintained its ‘Buy’ rating and ₹375 target price despite describing the results as weaker than expected. Food delivery performed in line with estimates, but quick commerce losses exceeded expectations. It nevertheless noted early signs of a recovery in growth.

HSBC maintained its ‘Hold’ rating but cut its target price to ₹240 from ₹315. It said improvements in Instamart’s operating metrics were insufficient to build confidence in Swiggy’s long-term plans, while flagging food delivery market share losses and intensifying competition.

Macquarie maintained its ‘Underperform’ rating with a target price of ₹230, citing negative cash flow and intense competition. It said continued spending on pricing and network expansion, alongside monetisation pressures, could delay profitability.

Bank of America retained its ‘Neutral’ rating but cut its target price to ₹245 from ₹275. It noted that Swiggy’s food delivery GOV grew 18% YoY, compared with Zomato’s 21.5%. The brokerage also flagged potential cannibalisation of Swiggy’s main food delivery business by its affordable-meals offering Toing, adding that Blinkit’s performance was increasing pressure on Instamart to demonstrate a path to profitability.

Instamart’s Profitability Roadmap

Instamart reported operating revenue of ₹1,306 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 33% YoY and 6% QoQ. Its segment loss widened to ₹764 Cr from ₹739 Cr a year earlier and ₹651 Cr in the preceding quarter.

Despite the increase in absolute adjusted EBITDA losses, its adjusted EBITDA margin improved marginally to -9.7% of GOV from -9.8% in Q1 FY27.

Swiggy said it believes Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA losses peaked in Q2 FY27. It expects double-digit sequential NOV growth in Q3 FY27, alongside an improvement of around 100 basis points in adjusted EBITDA margin.

Instamart added 1.3 Mn average monthly transacting users during the quarter, taking the total to 14.8 Mn. Orders rose 29% YoY to 130.3 Mn, while net average order value increased 4% to ₹506.

The platform added 69 dark stores, expanding its network to 1,240 stores across 133 cities.

Swiggy also plans to begin shifting Instamart to an inventory-led model by mid-Q3 FY27, with the transition expected to take two to three quarters. Under this model, the business will own the inventory it sells.

Swiggy expects the transition to improve Instamart’s contribution margin by around 80 basis points and shorten its working capital cycle by eight to 10 days.

Meanwhile, food delivery operating revenue rose 22% YoY to ₹2,338 Cr, while segment profit increased 39% to ₹349 Cr.

“Our food delivery business delivered its highest ever profits and margins while we continue to unlock new category growth through Toing, our standalone offering for affordable meals,” Swiggy cofounder, MD and group CEO Sriharsha Majety said.
